title: Task 2 — Structure & the Five Essay Types
summary: Task 2 is worth two-thirds of your Writing band, and the single biggest thing that sinks a script is answering the wrong question. Get the structure automatic and the question type right, and half the battle is already won.

seo.title: IELTS Task 2 Essay Structure & 5 Types Explained | Vidaara
seo.description: Master IELTS Writing Task 2: the universal essay structure, the five question types, a 5-minute planning method and a full band-9 model essay.

objectives: Build the universal Task 2 structure so it becomes automatic under pressure
Identify all five common question types from their wording
Plan a full essay in five minutes before you write a word
Avoid the off-task trap that caps so many scripts at band 5

blocks.html:
Task 2 asks for a minimum of 250 words in about 40 minutes, and it carries roughly two-thirds of your Writing band. The prompt is identical for Academic and General Training candidates — an essay responding to an argument, a problem, or a question. So whatever version you're sitting, this lesson matters more than any other in the Writing test.

Here's the part most people underestimate. The examiner isn't looking for a clever or original argument. They're checking whether you did four things: answered the whole question, organised your ideas, used a range of accurate vocabulary, and controlled your grammar. A plain, well-organised essay that answers the exact question beats a dazzling one that drifts off-topic. Every time.

The universal structure

Almost every high-scoring Task 2 essay uses the same four-part skeleton. It works across all five question types with only small adjustments. Learn it once, and you stop spending exam minutes wondering how to begin.

ParagraphWhat goes in itRough length
IntroductionParaphrase the question (don't copy it word for word), then one sentence that states your position or outlines what the essay will do.2–3 sentences
Body 1Topic sentence (your first main idea) → explanation of why it's true → a specific example.4–6 sentences
Body 2Topic sentence (your second main idea) → explanation → example. Same shape as Body 1.4–6 sentences
ConclusionRestate your position in fresh words and sum up the two ideas. No new arguments, no new examples.1–2 sentences

blocks.title: The T-E-E pattern is your body-paragraph engine
blocks.html: Every body paragraph follows the same rhythm: Topic sentence, Explanation, Example. The topic sentence names the idea, the explanation answers "why?" or "how?", and the example makes it concrete. If a body paragraph feels thin, it's almost always the explanation or example that's missing — not the vocabulary.

The five question types

Every Task 2 prompt belongs to one of five families. The wording tells you which one you're looking at, and each family asks you to do something slightly different. Misread the family and you can write a fluent, error-free essay that still scores band 5, because you answered a question the examiner didn't ask.

TypeTell-tale wordingWhat it requires
1. Opinion (Agree / Disagree)"To what extent do you agree or disagree?" / "Do you agree with this statement?"Take one clear position and defend it throughout. Both body paragraphs support your stance (or one concession + one main reason).
2. Discussion"Discuss both views and give your own opinion."One body paragraph per view, then make YOUR opinion explicit. Missing your own view caps Task Response.
3. Problem–Solution / Causes–Solutions"What problems does this cause and how can they be solved?" / "What are the causes and what measures can address them?"One paragraph on the problems (or causes), one on realistic solutions clearly linked to them.
4. Advantages–Disadvantages"What are the advantages and disadvantages?" / "Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?"Cover both sides. If asked whether one outweighs the other, you MUST give a verdict and hold it.
5. Two-part / Direct questionTwo separate direct questions, e.g. "Why is this happening? What can be done about it?"Answer BOTH questions — ideally one body paragraph each. Skipping one halves your Task Response.

blocks.title: Reading the question wrong is the #1 band killer
blocks.html: A huge share of band-5 scripts aren't weak in English — they're off-task. The classic slip is turning a discussion prompt ("discuss both views") into an opinion essay where you argue one side and ignore the other. Or answering "do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?" by listing pros and cons without ever saying which side wins. Before you plan a single idea, underline the instruction words and say to yourself, in plain language, exactly what the question wants you to do.

blocks.title: Plan your essay in five minutes
items: Minute 1 — Decode the question. Read it twice. Identify the type from the wording above and underline the exact instruction ("agree or disagree", "both views", "outweigh").
Minute 2 — Decide your answer. For opinion/discussion, fix your position now. For problem–solution, name the problem you'll tackle. Commit before you brainstorm, so every idea serves your line.
Minute 3 — Two ideas, two paragraphs. Jot one main idea per body paragraph. Two well-developed ideas beat four rushed ones every time.
Minute 4 — One example each. Beside each idea, note a specific example — a real trend, a plausible everyday scenario, a named field. Vague essays lack examples, not adjectives.
Minute 5 — Plan the paraphrase. Rephrase the prompt's key nouns and verbs in your head. This becomes your opening sentence and saves you freezing on the blank first line.

blocks.html:
What a band-9 answer actually looks like

Below is a worked introduction and first body paragraph for an opinion prompt. Notice how the introduction paraphrases the question and states a clear position in two sentences, and how the body paragraph runs cleanly through topic sentence, explanation, and example without a wasted word.

blocks.title: Turning a prompt into a plan
blocks.prompt: Some people believe that unpaid community service should be a compulsory part of high school programmes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
blocks.answer: Type: Opinion (agree/disagree). Position: Strongly agree. Body 1: Service builds skills school subjects can't teach — teamwork, responsibility (example: students running a food drive learn logistics and empathy). Body 2: It strengthens the link between young people and their communities, reducing isolation (example: volunteering at care homes bridges generations).
blocks.explain: The plan fixes the question type and a firm position first, then assigns one distinct idea to each body paragraph with a concrete example attached. There's no overlap between the two ideas, which keeps the essay from repeating itself — a common band-6 problem.

blocks.title: Band-9 opinion essay (worked example)
blocks.html:
It is increasingly argued that secondary schools should require students to complete unpaid community work as a condition of graduating. I strongly agree with this proposal, both because such work develops abilities that academic lessons cannot, and because it reconnects young people with the communities they live in.

The most compelling reason to make service compulsory is that it teaches practical skills no textbook can. When teenagers organise a local food drive or coach younger children, they must coordinate with others, manage their time and take genuine responsibility for an outcome that affects real people. These experiences build teamwork and resilience in a way that a graded exam never will. A student who has spent a term helping run a neighbourhood recycling scheme, for instance, has learned to negotiate, delegate and follow through — precisely the qualities employers and universities say they value most.

A second, and less obvious, benefit is social rather than personal. Many young people today move through school with little meaningful contact with anyone outside their own age group. Requiring service deliberately breaks that bubble. A teenager who volunteers weekly at a care home comes to understand the lives of much older people, while an adult resident gains company and attention they might otherwise lack. Multiplied across a whole cohort, these small encounters weaken the isolation that increasingly divides generations, and they remind students that they are part of something larger than their own results.

In conclusion, I firmly believe compulsory community service belongs in every high school programme. It equips students with real-world skills and knits them more tightly into their communities — outcomes that fully justify the modest time it demands.
annotations: The introduction paraphrases the prompt ("unpaid community work as a condition of graduating") instead of copying it, and states a clear, unhedged position — the examiner knows exactly where the writer stands.
Each body paragraph opens with a signposting topic sentence ("The most compelling reason...", "A second... benefit"), so the structure is visible at a glance.
Both paragraphs run T-E-E: idea, explanation, then a specific example (food drive, recycling scheme, care home) that grounds the claim.
Less common vocabulary is used precisely — 'cohort', 'delegate', 'resilience', 'weaken the isolation' — without straining for showy words.
The conclusion restates the position in fresh wording and names both ideas, adding nothing new. It signals a finished argument, not an abandoned one.

blocks.title: Structure first, flair later
blocks.html: If you take one habit from this lesson, make it the five-minute plan. Candidates who plan finish with time to proofread and almost never wander off-task. Once the skeleton is automatic, we'll fit each question type to it: start with the two most common — the opinion and discussion essays.

faqs.q: How many paragraphs should a Task 2 essay have?
faqs.a: Four is the safe standard: an introduction, two body paragraphs, and a conclusion. Two well-developed body paragraphs almost always score better than three or four thin ones, because each idea gets a proper explanation and example.

faqs.q: Do I have to give my own opinion in every Task 2 essay?
faqs.a: Not every type asks for one. Opinion and discussion essays require a clear personal position, and problem–solution or advantages–disadvantages essays may not. Always match what you write to the exact instruction in the prompt — that is what Task Response rewards.

faqs.q: How long should I spend planning?
faqs.a: About five minutes of your forty. It feels like a lot when the clock is running, but a quick plan stops you drifting off-task, prevents mid-essay panic, and usually leaves you time to proofread — all of which lift your band.

faqs.q: What is the most common reason people lose marks in Task 2?
faqs.a: Answering the wrong question. Many candidates write fluent English but misread the type — turning a 'discuss both views' prompt into a one-sided argument, or forgetting to give the verdict an 'outweigh' question demands. Read the instruction words carefully before you plan.
